2.text: The Taˊn˙ñɪt of these stories are either the Russian Cossacks, or more

3.text: frequently, the Reindeer Koryak. The Reindeer Chukchee were obliged to

4.text: defend themselves against the invasion of the Cossacks, and even succeeded

5.text: in defeating Major Pavlutsky and his troops.¹ Still the remembrance of this

6.text: war is not so strong as might be expected; and the tales relating to it are

7.text: mostly short, and poor in details. Those that relate to Koryak wars, on the

8.text: contrary, abound in vivid episodes. Some of the tales relating to the wars

9.text: with the Russians represent simply the stories of the Koryak war-cycle, changed

10.text: and adapted to a new use. The details relating to the arms and the ways

11.text: of the new enemy are inserted; but the Chukchee heroes are described in the

12.text: same manner, and even their names are unchanged.

13.text: War Heroes. — I have already mentioned that in war-stories a number

14.text: of warriors figure who are described individually. Their names are quite

15.text: popular, and appear in various combinations.² All these belong to the Koryak

16.text: war-cycle. The most remarkable thing is, that one of them is mentioned as

17.text: the chief and leader. His name is Lauˊtɪ-lɪwaˊlɪn, which means “head-nodder.”

18.text: This name is given to him because he gives the signal for attack by a nod

19.text: of his head. It is curious to know that this explanation is half-forgotten.

20.text: Sometimes I received the answer that the name of Head-Nodder sprang from

21.text: the habit of nodding his head while moving with reindeer over the rough

22.text: ground of the tundra. The wars with Taˊn˙ñɪt evidently tended to develop

23.text: the office of a military chief, though the ordinary conditions of Chukchee life

24.text: are too simple for such an institution. The development did not proceed

25.text: very far; and as soon as the wars ceased, it vanished, and even the signific-

26.text: ance of the name was forgotten.

27.text: Head-Nodder is described as one who gathers warriors for an expedition.

28.text: His voice is thick and strong. When the women of a Taˊn˙ñɪn fortress be-

29.text: sieged by Chukchee hear his voice, they speedily kill their own children, and

30.text: the young girls kill themselves. His companions are Eᵋleˊnnut and Aiñaˊɪrg̣ɪn.

31.text: The latter name means “the clamoring one,” and even now is frequently met

32.text: with among the Chukchee. Eᵋleˊnnut is described as the assistant of Head-

35.text: answers, “I will be thy in-the-armpit-being-little bird.” After that, they rush

36.text: to the assault, shoulder to shoulder.
